States Data≠Knowledge (a database row/document/embedding/log entry is data; knowledge requires semantic interpretation, illustrated by an ADR-approval string needing subject/authority/timestamp/rationale/status/provenance to become a Decision) and demonstrates via experiment that a field value like status=APPROVED is not sufficient semantic evidence absent WhoApproved/UnderWhichAuthority/When/WhatWasApproved/WhatEvidenceSupportsIt. Defines the semantic object tuple Concept=(Identity,Meaning,State,Invariants,Relationships,Authority,Provenance) and lists ten candidate concepts (evidence/observations/claims/decisions/rules/architecture/agents/changes/findings/verification), with ConceptMention≠ConceptImplementation (four classes containing the word Evidence establish terminology, not a coherent Evidence domain) and per-concept semantic definition reconstruction from actual implementation rather than assumed definition, illustrated by a Module-A-treats-evidence-as-source-document vs Module-B-treats-evidence-as-runtime-observation semantic collision (OBS) with the Meaning boundary caveat that Evidence_A≠Evidence_B can be legitimate across genuinely distinct contexts, the problem arising only when treated as the same concept without explicit translation. Defines a bounded context as existing where a coherent semantic model owns Concepts+Rules+Invariants+Language, with BoundedContext≠Directory (an 'evidence/' directory containing only file parsing/OCR/embeddings may be an ingestion component, not an Evidence bounded context). Reframes semantic ownership as 'who owns the meaning' not 'who stores the record' (an EvidenceRepository stores; an EvidenceDomain defines meaning and validity; the validating-rules service among three evidence-writing services is the stronger semantic-owner candidate), with Invariant->Owner as the strongest ownership-identification technique (the component enforcing Approved⇒AuthorityPresent likely owns the decision invariant) and state-transition authority as revealing governance boundary (any component able to transition Candidate->Authoritative directly is a potential semantic/governance defect, OBS/VIOLATION). Covers stable semantic identity (filename-as-identity is fragile identity, OBS), provenance connecting KnowledgeObject to seven possible origin types (with a no-source-or-provenance claim flagged PARTIAL/weak knowledge object), the True≠Authoritative distinction (an AI recommendation is not an ArchitectureDecision) and the Suggestion->Review->Decision->AuthoritativeState authority-transition model, temporal semantics (Knowledge(t); Current/Historical/Superseded, both v1.0 and v1.2 architecture rules remaining historically meaningful with only v1.2 current) and Knowledge-version≠SourceCodeVersion (knowledge can evolve independently of software releases), conflict semantics (Claim_A≠Claim_B must not automatically resolve to newest-wins; KnowledgeOS should record Conflict with sources/dates/authorities/scope, and Conflict itself is useful knowledge via Conflict->Finding->Resolution, silently overwriting one side destroying organizational history), an eight-verb semantic relationship vocabulary (supports/contradicts/supersedes/derivedFrom/implements/verifies/authorizes/violates) called more important than simple foreign keys (an untyped pointer between records is a weak knowledge graph, PARTIAL), the semantic graph G_K=(V_K,E_K) with a worked Architecture-Rule->implementedBy->Component->verifiedBy->Test->produces->Evidence->observedAt->Runtime chain explicitly called fundamentally different from a document repository, semantic-ownership-via-DDD-cluster (Meaning+Rules+Lifecycle+Ownership forming a coherent cluster around Evidence/Source/Observation/Verification as an EvidenceContextCandidate), context-boundary-through-translation (Governance's Finding vs Runtime's Alert modeled as RuntimeAlert->GovernanceFinding rather than pretending Alert=Finding) and an explicit anti-corruption-layer pattern (ExternalModel->Translation->KnowledgeOSModel, e.g. Mapping(JiraIssue,ChangeRequest) rather than JiraIssue=ChangeRequest), a semantic ownership matrix template (Concept x Meaning/Invariants/Data owner/Semantic owner/External source, all cells deliberately '?'), the semantic orphan pattern (Meaning exists but Owner=Unknown, illustrated by 'Knowledge item' used across five modules with no identifiable invariant or owner, OBS) and semantic duplicate pattern (two concepts with identical meaning/lifecycle/API behavior, e.g. KnowledgeRecord vs KnowledgeItem, OBS), semantic fragmentation as potentially the most serious pattern (OneConcept->ManyOwners, e.g. Decision independently owned by ServiceA/ServiceB/AgentMemory, creating ambiguity about truth, illustrated by three independent current-architecture-decision representations classified DRIFT) resolved not necessarily by a single database but by the requirement of one authoritative semantic owner with legitimate physical projections elsewhere (API View/Search Index/Agent Context all projecting one Authoritative Decision, not competing authorities) validated by Source->Version->Freshness cache-validity tracking and stale-projection detection (agent cache retaining version 4 after the authoritative decision moves to version 5 = ProjectionStale), explicitly connecting back to the pointer-layer principle in semantic terms (Agent->AuthoritativeKnowledge; agent memory may be Projection but not Authority) and extending it to governance authority itself needing an identifiable AuthorityHolder (Rule->Authority->AuthorityHolder, an unidentifiable authority = GovernanceGap), per-concept semantic lifecycles that must not be conflated (Claim: Proposed->Supported->Accepted->Superseded; Decision: Draft->Approved->Effective->Superseded; Finding: Open->Investigating->Remediating->Verified->Closed; a uniform ACTIVE|INACTIVE status across all knowledge objects flagged OBS as a semantic weakness since DecisionStatus is not FindingStatus), semantic invariants per concept (ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists; VerifiedEvidence⇒VerificationEventExists; SupersededRule⇒ReplacementExists where required by policy) with a database-permits-VerifiedEvidence-without-VerificationEvent enforcement-gap experiment, the requirement to identify WHERE each invariant is actually enforced (domain code/application service/database constraint/policy engine/workflow/CI/runtime/human process, with a README-only invariant traceability = potential destruction of the semantic core) generalized into the semantic-core test ('if this component disappeared, would KnowledgeOS lose the meaning of its knowledge, or merely a knowledge-oriented tooling).

summary: Step 113 reaches the central architectural question -- what is the irreducible semantic core of KnowledgeOS -- distinguishing a platform with many 'knowledge' features from one with a coherent knowledge model. Restates the semantic-core hypothesis Evidence->Claim->Decision->Authority->Action->Observation with cross-cutting Provenance/TemporalValidity as still a hypothesis pending implementation confirmation, and introduces a ten-question falsification principle (existence/stable identity/defined meaning/lifecycle/invariants/relationships/identifiable ownership/persisted representation/implemented behavior/verification) such that a concept failing most questions should not be treated as part of the actual semantic core. Works through ten candidate concepts each with a minimal semantic-definition tuple and falsifying/clarifying experiments: (1) Evidence=(Identity,Source,Content/Observation,Timestamp,Provenance,Context[,VerificationStatus]) with the Artifact->Evidence semantic-transformation distinction (a file is an artifact until the system establishes its evidentiary role; Artifact!=Evidence but Artifact->Evidence) and three competing evidence-ownership models (EvidenceAuthority/EvidenceAggregator/EvidenceProcessingPlatform) to be resolved by implementation; (2) Observation as something observed with no interpretation yet (Observation-supports->Claim, the observation itself remaining distinct, valuable for auditability); (3) Claim as a proposition asserted true within a context, not yet a decision (an LLM's 'the system appears compliant' is an AI-generated claim, not automatically authoritative) with a five-state lifecycle (Proposed/Supported/Accepted/Disputed/Superseded) conditional on implementation representation; (4) Decision=(Subject,Choice,Authority,Rationale,Evidence,EffectiveDate) stronger than a claim, with Decision!=Recommendation requiring identifiable Authority(Decision) (a document recommendation is not a decision; an agent's 'the board should approve this' is a recommendation, not the board's decision); (5) Authority=(Actor,Role,Scope,Rule,Validity), explicitly not merely a user ID (an 'admin' user identity does not automatically equal ArchitectureAuthority) with a worked four-row authority matrix (Architecture/Implementation/Security exception/Agent action decision types with their authorities and scopes) requiring evidenced ownership; (6) Action=(Actor,Intent,Target,Change,Time,Authorization) important because KnowledgeOS participates in engineering workflows, with Action->Actor/Intent/Evidence provenance requirements (Actor=AgentIdentity for AI) and a PARTIAL-classified experiment where file changes are logged without recorded agent identity (incomplete action provenance); (7) Verification=(Rule,Input,Method,Result,Evidence,Timestamp) distinct from Evidence (a passing test is TestResult evidence of verification but Test!=Verification unless the semantic model explicitly treats it that way); (8) Finding as Expected!=Observed, with the sharp caution TestFailure!=Finding without interpretation (a failed test may be infrastructure failure/flaky test/developer error/actual conformance violation, not automatically a governance finding); (9) Rule as Allowed/Forbidden/Required constraining behavior (e.g. Agent-cannot-access-ProductionDB), connecting architecture to deterministic assurance, with a documented-but-unenforced-status experiment; (10) Architecture=(Components,Relationships,Constraints,Decisions,Views,Validity) modeled as knowledge while explicitly avoiding circularity (KnowledgeOS manages architectural knowledge without architecture being the semantic root of ALL knowledge). Establishes provenance and temporal validity as cross-cutting concerns applying to every semantic object (Evidence/Claim/Decision/Action/Observation all ->Provenance), with a worked experiment showing identical-text knowledge objects from ArchitectureBoard versus an LLM cannot be treated as semantically equivalent solely by text identity, and a ValidFrom/ValidUntil cross-cutting concern (an agent retrieving a rule superseded yesterday should not treat it as current, motivating semantic retrieval beyond vector similarity). Presents the candidate semantic core as a graph (Authority-authorizes->Decision-{supportedBy->Evidence, resultsIn->Action->produces->Observation-derivedFrom->Source}) with cross-cutting Provenance/TemporalValidity/Identity, explicitly flagged as requiring empirical confirmation (search for explicit entities/schemas/relationships/state transitions/persistence/APIs/verification mechanisms) since SemanticCore_actual may not equal SemanticCore_target. Defines three possible outcomes -- A Explicit semantic core (Strong, first-class representations), B Distributed semantic core (Partial, concepts exist across several mechanisms), C Emergent semantic core (Weak, concepts inferable from documents/logs/workflows but not explicitly modeled) -- illustrated by a no-Claim-entity-but-claims-implied-elsewhere experiment yielding possible emergent claim semantics, with the explicit caution not to invent a Claim domain object merely because the architecture model suggests one. Introduces semantic core minimality as a formal anti-overengineering principle Core_minimal=argmin(Model) subject to Model⊢ObservedBehavior, illustrated by an experiment where Artifact+Observation+Decision+Evidence already explain all current behavior, so a separate Claim entity would add no explanatory value and should not be introduced merely for conceptual elegance. Distinguishes semantic core from feature catalog (search/ingestion/embeddings/agent-integration/governance/audit are capabilities; the semantic core asks what concepts give them coherent meaning, e.g. Search supports Retrieve(KnowledgeObject), Embeddings support Similarity(KnowledgeObject), Governance supports Authorize(KnowledgeObject), Audit supports Prove(Action)) via four component-removal thought experiments (removing vector search leaves identity/provenance intact = core survives; removing provenance destroys traceability = significant degradation; removing authority semantics collapses recommendation/decision distinction = governance semantics collapse; removing temporal validity makes superseded rules indistinguishable from current = freshness/integrity unreliable). Proposes six candidate semantic-core invariants S1-S6 (EveryAuthoritativeDecision->Authority; EveryMaterialClaim->Provenance; EveryVerification->Evidence; EveryAgentAction->AgentIdentity; CurrentKnowledge->TemporalValidity; Projection->AuthoritativeSource), explicitly hypotheses pending implementation confirmation. Defines a semantic truth hierarchy RawData->Observation->Evidence->Claim->Decision (progressively stronger semantic commitments) with Authority determining organizational bindingness, with the important caution that this is NOT a linear pipeline but a graph (a Decision can itself become Evidence for a later decision; an Observation can trigger a Finding directly without becoming a Claim first). Presents the full candidate semantic graph diagram (Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Claim->Evidence with named edges) explicitly as a target model, not yet a claim about actual code, and the decisive reconstruction test asking for each edge whether it is represented anywhere in the actual system (foreign key/API relation/event/domain object/metadata/graph edge/workflow/test/runtime record), with a SemanticGap experiment (architecture specifies Decision-supportedBy->Evidence but implementation has no such relationship) and a DocumentedRelationship-vs-MachineReadableSemanticRelationship distinction (a relationship existing only in Markdown text is documented, not machine-readable). Illustrates machine-readable semantics via example decision fields (supporting_evidence[]/authority/effective_from/supersedes) flagged as an implementation question, and reframes semantic retrieval from document-similarity search ('find documents containing X') to genuine semantic query ('find authoritative decisions concerning X, their supporting evidence, current validity, and unresolved findings'), formalized as Find(Decision,subject=X,validNow=True,authority=ArchitectureBoard) combined with Include(Evidence,Findings,SupersededDecisions), with the agent-consequence principle that an agent should receive CurrentAuthoritativeKnowledge rather than TopKSimilarDocuments (the latter useful retrieval infrastructure, the former a genuine knowledge operating model). Closes with a Step 113 verdict defining a falsifiable semantic-core model (Evidence+Observation+Claim+Decision+Authority+Action+Provenance+TemporalValidity with semantic relationships) while explicitly refusing to claim all of these exist in the current implementation, yielding the honest dual status TargetSemanticCore=Defined / ActualSemanticCore=ToBeReconstructed, and previews Step 114 (Semantic Core Evidence Test: a strict eight-concept x seven-column [Code/Schema/API/Tests/Runtime/Owner/Verdict] evidence matrix where every non-unknown cell must have evidence, determining whether KnowledgeOS is a true semantic knowledge platform or an engineering/AI platform whose knowledge model is still emerging).
contribution_assessment: Extends the semantic-ownership reconstruction model (S1011/Step 112) into a fully worked, falsifiable semantic-core hypothesis for KnowledgeOS. Contributes a rigorous ten-question falsification principle for admitting any candidate concept into the semantic core (existence through verification), directly operationalizing the project's broader anti-overclaiming discipline (Steps 108/109/112) at the concept level rather than the component level. Works through ten fully-specified candidate concepts (Evidence, Observation, Claim, Decision, Authority, Action, Verification, Finding, Rule, Architecture), each given a minimal semantic tuple and at least one falsifying or clarifying experiment, producing several durable, reusable distinctions: Artifact≠Evidence (with the semantic-transformation arrow Artifact->Evidence, and three competing candidate evidence-ownership architectures -- EvidenceAuthority/EvidenceAggregator/EvidenceProcessingPlatform -- left for implementation to resolve); Observation-supports->Claim keeping the observation itself distinct for auditability; Decision≠Recommendation requiring identifiable Authority(Decision) (extending Step 112's True≠Authoritative and Step 108's AI-vs-deterministic-assurance principle into the decision-authority domain, with the sharp example that an agent recommending board approval has not thereby created the board's decision); Authority as a structured (Actor,Role,Scope,Rule,Validity) tuple explicitly not reducible to a user identity; TestFailure≠Finding without interpretation (a failed test may be infrastructure noise, not a governance finding) -- a materially important safeguard against naive automated-finding generation; and Architecture-as-knowledge explicitly modeled while avoiding circularity (architecture is managed knowledge, not necessarily knowledge's semantic root). Establishes provenance and temporal validity as formally cross-cutting concerns spanning every semantic object, with a striking worked example (identical text from ArchitectureBoard versus an LLM cannot be treated as semantically equivalent purely on textual identity) that operationalizes the True≠Authoritative distinction at the provenance level. Presents the full candidate semantic graph as an explicit target model (not a claim about actual code) and defines the decisive reconstruction test -- for every edge, is the relationship represented anywhere in the actual system via nine possible evidence types -- directly extending Step 109's evidence-classification apparatus to the semantic-relationship level, producing a concrete SemanticGap finding pattern and the DocumentedRelationship-vs-MachineReadableSemanticRelationship distinction. Defines three mutually exclusive outcome categories for how (or whether) the semantic core is actually represented -- Explicit/Strong, Distributed/Partial, Emergent/Weak -- paired with an explicit anti-invention discipline (do not create a Claim domain object merely because the target model suggests one) and a formalized semantic-core-minimality principle Core_minimal=argmin(Model) subject to Model⊢ObservedBehavior, a genuinely novel anti-overengineering criterion for this reconstruction track, demonstrated by an experiment where four existing concepts (Artifact/Observation/Decision/Evidence) already fully explain observed behavior, making a fifth Claim entity explanatorily redundant. Distinguishes the semantic core from a mere feature catalog by showing each capability (search/embeddings/governance/audit) is only meaningful in terms of an underlying object it operates on, validated through four component-removal thought experiments that rank Provenance and Authority as more architecturally load-bearing than retrieval infrastructure like vector search. Proposes six candidate semantic-core invariants S1-S6 (each explicitly a hypothesis pending confirmation) and a semantic truth hierarchy RawData->Observation->Evidence->Claim->Decision with the crucial caution that it forms a graph, not a linear pipeline (a Decision can become Evidence for a later Decision; an Observation can directly trigger a Finding). Closes by reframing semantic retrieval itself as an architectural capability -- contrasting naive document-similarity search against a genuine structured semantic query (Find(Decision,...) combined with Include(Evidence,Findings,SupersededDecisions)) and the agent-consequence principle CurrentAuthoritativeKnowledge vs TopKSimilarDocuments, which gives concrete operational content to the abstract semantic-core hypothesis. Delivers a Step 113 verdict that explicitly refuses to conflate the defined target model with implementation reality (TargetSemanticCore=Defined / ActualSemanticCore=ToBeReconstructed) and previews Step 114's strict, evidence-only eight-concept conformance matrix, framed as making testable the central question of whether KnowledgeOS is a true semantic knowledge platform or an engineering/AI platform whose knowledge model is still emerging.

summary: Step 114 tests the Step 113 semantic-core hypothesis (Evidence+Observation+Claim+Decision+Authority+Action+Provenance+TemporalValidity) against the actual KnowledgeOS implementation, asking strictly which concepts are actually first-class in the current system -- not which appear in documentation, not which 'should' exist, not which an LLM can infer; only actual-implementation evidence counts. Defines T(C)=(Code,Schema,API,Tests,Runtime,Owner,Relations) as the seven-dimension evidence test per concept, classified into six grades S0 (terminology only) through S5 (governed), with the key distinction that S1 (represented) does not imply S5 (governed) -- a Decision table can exist without a genuine decision-governance model. Works through each of the eight core concepts with dimension-specific questions and worked experiments: Evidence (code/schema/API/tests/runtime/ownership/relations questions, with the verdict rule that only alignment across several dimensions yields Evidence=FirstClassSemanticConcept, otherwise Evidence=TechnicalMetadata/Artifact); Observation (potential sources Runtime/CI/Git/Agent/Human, the critical ObservedFact-vs-Interpretation distinction, and an Observation=Partial experiment where a bare status=FAILED lacks source/time/context); Claim (distinguished from raw document/observation/recommendation/decision, with an AI-agent assertion example explicitly not a first-class KnowledgeOS claim absent a claim object); Decision (the Recommendation-vs-Decision distinction as one of the most important semantic boundaries, with a DecisionSemantics=Weak experiment where a generated recommendation and an approved decision share one undifferentiated table); Authority (harder to establish than role -- a user_id+role pair does not implement decision authority; requires Authority->Scope->Permission->DecisionType, with a ROLE_ARCHITECT-without-decision-restriction experiment showing role exists but authority semantics do not); Action (requiring Who+What+Why+When+AgainstWhat+UnderWhichAuthority reconstructable, with an ActionProvenance=Partial experiment where only 'file changed' is logged without agent identity/command/intent/authorization); Provenance (Provenance(X)=Source+Actor+Time+Transformation+Context, called possibly the most important cross-cutting concept, with a source_url-only experiment establishing partial source attribution short of complete provenance); Temporal validity (CreatedAt≠ValidFrom, illustrated by a created_at-only object lacking effective/supersession semantics). Extends to relationship-level testing: the semantic relationship test (Evidence-supports->Claim, Claim-informs->Decision, Decision-authorizes->Action) with an experiment showing two unconnected Decision/Evidence records leave Decision<->Evidence semantics unestablished; the semantic edge test requiring evidence of relationship/direction/meaning/lifecycle for every edge, with an evidence_ids[] field on Decision yielding only S1/S2 (not automatically S3, since enforcement that the IDs represent genuine supporting evidence remains unverified); the sharp Relationship-semantics-vs-foreign-keys distinction (A.id->B.id does not necessarily mean A-supports->B, illustrated by a decision_id-in-an-audit-table experiment that does not prove evidentiary support); the semantic lifecycle test (Draft->Reviewed->Approved->Effective->Superseded template) with a DRAFT/APPROVED-enum-without-transition-rules experiment graded S1, and a Draft->Effective-rejected-without-approval experiment graded S2/S3 depending on verification; the semantic invariant test (ApprovedDecision⇒AuthorityExists as an executable assert) with a SpecifiedInvariant-vs-ImplementedInvariant distinction (an ADR-only rule is specified, not implemented) and cross-concept invariants (Decision->Evidence, Action->Decision/Authorization) valued above isolated field validation, illustrated by an OBS/VIOL-classified agent-action-without-authorization-decision experiment. Proposes the stronger target semantic-authority chain Authority->Decision->Action->Observation->Evidence with Provenance connecting each step as a complete organizational feedback loop, paired with an explicit epistemic-discipline warning against prematurely claiming 'KnowledgeOS has this architecture' -- correctly stated only as the hypothesis being tested. Presents the formal semantic-core evidence matrix (eight concepts x Representation/Behavior/Verification/Runtime/Authority/Relationships, all cells '?') as the central empirical artifact, an ordinal evidence-grade scale 0=No evidence through 6=Governed (Grade(C)∈[0,6]) with three worked grading experiments (documentation-only=1; code+tests but no runtime=4; implemented+tested+production-demonstrated=5, +ownership/governance=6), the deliberately-deferred SemanticCoreStrength weighted-average formula explicitly NOT to be calculated yet (Vector>Scalar: a high average of Evidence=5/Authority=1 could conceal a critical weakness, so individual dimensions must be retained rather than collapsed), semantic completeness as presence of essential relationship edges (Evidence->Claim->Decision->Action->Observation) rather than raw entity count, illustrated by an all-eight-concepts-exist-but-no-Decision->Authority-edge experiment leaving the core incomplete, and the Core_minimum concept (a semantic core defined by the minimum relationships necessary to preserve system meaning, not by entity count), illustrated by a documents+embeddings+search+chat-history+vector-retrieval system explicitly lacking Authority/Decision semantics -- 'a sophisticated knowledge retrieval system, but the semantic core remains weak.' Draws the decisive Knowledge Retrieval Platform (Documents->Embeddings->Retrieval) vs Knowledge Operating System (Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->UpdatedKnowledge) distinction, the latter possessing organizational state and control semantics, visualized as a full feedback-loop diagram (Knowledge->Evidence->Reasoning->Decision->Action->Observation->NewEvidence->Knowledge) explicitly called the operating-system loop being tested for. Extends this to agent integration (Agent->Reasoning/Recommendation/Action with authority remaining explicit; Recommendation->Human/PolicyDecision never Recommendation=Decision) and autonomous agent action requiring DelegatedAuthority (HumanAuthority-delegates->AgentAuthority; AgentAction->DelegatedAuthority), illustrated by an agent-with-production-credentials-but-no-delegation-record experiment showing technical capability without established semantic authority, called extremely important for AI governance. Distinguishes ModelOutput from DecisionEvidence (an LLM's own verification claim absent tool execution is an UnverifiedAIAssertion) versus tool-backed verification (Agent->VerificationTool->DeterministicResult->Evidence, consistent with the earlier deterministic-assurance architecture) illustrated by a PASS-graded architecture-test-with-full-evidence-bundle experiment. Formulates a KnowledgeOS identity test (whether major capabilities like Search/AgentHooks/Governance/Audit/VectorDB connect through one coherent semantic model or are architecturally fragmented), illustrated by an every-subsystem-defines-knowledge-differently experiment classified DRIFT CANDIDATE/SemanticFragmentation, and states the two possible strongest findings symmetrically: KnowledgeObject=Document+Embedding with no Evidence/Decision/Authority model is a valuable (not failing) finding that the system is a knowledge retrieval/management platform whose richer semantic operating model is not yet implemented; conversely Evidence+Decision+Authority+Provenance+Verification with established relationships would be evidence the KnowledgeOS architecture is materially implemented. Closes with a Step 114 verdict stating ConceptualSemanticCore≠ProvenActualSemanticCore until the matrix is filled, marked READY FOR EMPIRICAL EXECUTION, and previews Step 115 (Semantic Graph Reconstruction: building the actual graph G_actual=(V_actual,E_actual) over real implementation concepts and relationships -- supports/implements/verifies/authorizes/produces/derivedFrom/supersedes/contradicts -- with the decisive experiment being whether an actual KnowledgeOS decision can be traced backward to authority/evidence and forward to action/observation, determining whether a genuine knowledge operating loop exists or precisely which semantic links are missing).

summary: Step 117 performs the first end-to-end architectural experiment, asking whether one real engineering change can be reconstructed from organizational intent to verified runtime reality and back into authoritative knowledge, via the target chain Intent->Decision->Authority->Implementation->Verification->Runtime->Evidence->Knowledge. States that tracing one representative change completely establishes the architecture has closed-loop mechanisms; a broken chain instead pinpoints exactly where the architecture currently stops. Defines the canonical engineering-change reconstruction object EC=(Intent,Decision,Authority,Change,Verification,Runtime,Evidence,Knowledge), explicitly not a new domain entity but a reconstruction structure for one real historical change. Works through all eight stages with concrete Nexus-upgrade-themed experiments: Intent (a bare 'upgrade Nexus' commit establishes ChangeOccurred, not WhyChangeWasRequired -- technical evidence only; a Jira ticket explicitly stating the unsupported-version rationale evidences Intent); Decision (Intent does not automatically create Decision -- 'Nexus needs modernization' differs materially from a specific upgrade-path decision; Document≠Decision, the document must actually establish the decision); Authority (Actor≠Authority, a Domain Architect's migration recommendation is not an AuthorizedDecision, while formal Architecture Board approval is Authority-authorizes->Decision if evidenced; AuthorityScope must be checked separately, e.g. the Board's architecture authority does not automatically extend to production operations); Implementation (Decision->ADR->Commit->BuildArtifact, with stronger ImplementationTrace=Strong when commit/PR/deployment records explicitly cross-reference the decision/ADR/change-request/build-artifact); Verification (a container starting proves only RuntimeStartup=True, not ArchitectureConformance=True, motivating four separated verification dimensions -- Functional/Architecture/Security/Operational -- since one successful test cannot represent all four, connected directly to the earlier deterministic-assurance principle Rule->DeterministicCheck->Result e.g. mechanically testing NoForbiddenDependency); Runtime (Verification->Runtime asking whether the deployed system became what was intended, illustrated by a DRIFT-classified build-artifact-says-v2-but-runtime-runs-v1 mismatch, and RuntimeInstance/ArtifactVersion/DeploymentID identity evidence); Observation (raw runtime facts like reachability/repository-count/data-size are observations, not conclusions -- 'container is healthy' is Observation, not automatically ArchitectureConformant) and Observation->Evidence interpretation (Observation-supports->Claim, illustrated by a rootless-Podman-requirement confirmed by runtime evidence); Updated Knowledge (Evidence->Knowledge, the change result becoming part of current organizational knowledge -- 'Nexus is now operated using the approved containerized architecture' -- more than a deployment log, with a Knowledge-synchronization-gap finding when deployment completes but KnowledgeOS never updates architecture state, RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState). Presents the canonical ten-row Engineering Traceability Record template (Intent/Decision/Authority/Implementation/Verification/Deployment/Runtime/Observation/Evidence/Knowledge x Question/Evidence) and four possible outcome classes -- A Complete (EndToEndTraceability), B Technically complete (strong Implementation->Runtime, weak Intent->Authority = TechnicalTraceability), C Governance complete (strong Decision->Implementation, weak runtime evidence = GovernanceTraceability), D Fragmented (TraceabilityFragmentation, unconnectable stages) -- reframing KnowledgeOS's value proposition from 'where is the architecture document' to 'why does the architecture exist, who authorized it, what implementation realizes it, and what evidence demonstrates continued conformance.' Extends this to agent use: an agent handling a change request should retrieve CurrentDecision/Authority/RelevantArchitecture/ImplementationConstraints/ExistingEvidence/KnownFindings before reasoning (a documentation-only retrieval is useful context but insufficient for CurrentAuthority), agent recommendations remaining AgentInference until board-approved into Decision, and Decision->DelegatedAuthority->AgentAction as the bridge between governance and AI engineering (illustrated by a Codex-PR-implementing-an-approved-decision trace Decision->CodexAction->PullRequest->Commit, provided references are preserved), with agent-run verification required to be Tool->DeterministicResult->Evidence rather than a prose 'looks good' summary. summary: Step 120 consolidates all prior architecture-conformance-arc experiments (Steps 101-119) into the smallest set of invariants whose violation would fundamentally change KnowledgeOS's nature, starting from the candidate Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus+TemporalValidity+DeterministicVerification+Traceability+Feedback. without it Recommendation can silently become Decision and AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth; a K2-VIOLATION-if-promoted experiment for an unauthorized agent-declared standard change; Actor≠Authority, Credential≠Authority, Role≠Authority unless the governance model explicitly maps them); K3 Epistemic status (KnowledgeOS MUST distinguish observed/verified/inferred/proposed/authoritative information, called perhaps the most important AI-specific invariant, illustrated by the textually-similar-but-epistemically-radically-different pair 'the service probably owns this database' vs 'the Architecture Board decided this service owns this database'; K4 Temporal validity (authoritative knowledge MUST have determinable temporal validity, at minimum Current vs Superseded; HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth illustrated by a 2024 decision possibly not representing 2026's current architecture; K6 Traceability (material engineering actions MUST be traceable to their governing intent/decision/authorization where governance requires it, Action->Decision; a K6-VIOLATION experiment for an untraceable production architecture change; the caveat that traceability does not mean bureaucracy -- RequiredTraceability(Action) depends on Risk+Scope+GovernanceClass, concerning required traceability not universal approval); K7 Feedback (material deviations between authoritative expected state and observed engineering reality MUST be capable of feeding back into governance and knowledge -- what makes the platform an operating system rather than a static repository;
